title: From Symmetry to Secrecy: Covariant Classical--Quantum Wiretap Channels
abstract: For classical--quantum wiretap channels with a transitive covariant input action, both output ensembles admit a description as unitary group orbits of fixed seed states. We use this structure to construct finite-block preprocessing schemes whose private information is an entropy difference evaluated at two distributions related by group convolution. Applying the construction to product groups allows correlations across any fixed number of channel uses. We give a sufficient condition for the associated uniform-input bound to equal the single-use private information. Constant-composition channel codes and universal$_2$ hashing achieve the resulting rates, with trace-distance leakage controlled by sandwiched Rényi information. For uniform outer randomization, the representation structure reduces the comparison-state optimization to Eve's invariant states. For the hybrid binary channel considered by Tikku, Berta and Renes, numerical optimization at three and four uses gives rates above our numerical estimate of the optimized noisy-repetition benchmark wherever that estimate is positive on the tested grid. The improvement comes from noise distributions beyond the family of independent physical flips and a symmetric logical flip. We also prove nonadditivity at an explicit channel parameter using a two-use encoder, an analytic single-use converse, and certified entropy bounds. Finally, we relate the hybrid model to binary phase-shift keying with a fixed receiver measurement.
summary: This paper develops theoretical bounds for the private information capacity of classical-quantum wiretap channels that possess specific symmetry properties (covariance). By leveraging group theory, the authors derive capacity formulas based on entropy differences calculated via group convolution. The work provides explicit examples of nonadditivity and compares achievable rates against standard benchmarks, advancing the understanding of secure quantum communication limits.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the private communication capacity of classical-quantum wiretap channels, focusing on how this capacity scales with multiple channel uses.
main_result: For covariant channels, the private information capacity is bounded below by expressions involving the convolution of an entropy difference functional derived from group theory.
method: The authors utilize group theory to characterize the channel structure via covariant actions, leading to bounds based on entropy differences calculated over group convolutions.
model_or_system: The model is a classical-quantum (cq) wiretap channel, where Alice transmits a classical message, and Bob and Eve receive quantum states. The analysis is specialized for channels exhibiting transitive covariance.
key_observables: Private information, quantified as $I(V; B) - I(V; E)$, and the entropy difference $\Delta(P) = H(ho_B(P)) - H(ho_E(P))$.
important_parameters: The number of channel uses ($n$), the channel parameter $p$ (in the hybrid binary case), and the structure of the underlying group $G$.
main_assumptions: The analysis heavily relies on the assumption that the input action is transitive and covariant, allowing the channel to be described by unitary group orbits.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the covariance property of the channel. Figure 7 compares the achieved rate ($	ext{Rach}_n$) against the repetition benchmark ($	ext{Rrep}_{\log n}$) for $n=2, 3, 4$ uses.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the group-theoretic structure of covariant channels, deriving bounds using preprocessing schemes based on entropy differences. It then applies these tools to specific models, including a hybrid binary channel, to demonstrate nonadditivity and compare achievable rates against theoretical benchmarks.
why_interesting: While focused on information theory, the use of group theory to constrain quantum channel behavior (covariance) provides powerful mathematical tools applicable to characterizing symmetries in open quantum systems or quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Covariance: permuting the classical input labels and conjugating the output states give the same channel outputs.
FIG. 2. A cq wiretap channel has one classical input and two quantum outputs. The coding problem compares the information available to Bob with the information leaked to Eve.
FIG. 3. The covariant preprocessing. Conditioned on V = v the input is the translate LvP1, whose entropies do not depend on v; the input marginal is the convolution P3 ∗P1.
FIG. 4. Encoding for the covariant bound. The hash seed determines the fiber from which the randomized index is drawn, and P1 supplies the sender-side group randomization.

FIG. 5. The single-use entropy difference f1(x, 0.05) −f2(x, 0.15) of the hybrid binary channel as a function of the input probability x. The minimum sits at a nonzero x, so the optimal sender noise is not a point mass: noisy preprocessing already pays off at a single channel use.
